mcqs.question: A perceptron uses a purely linear activation (or none at all). What is it mathematically equivalent to?
options: Logistic regression, capable only of separating data with a straight line
mcqs.explanation: With no non-linear activation, a perceptron's weighted sum plus bias is exactly the linear model behind logistic (or linear) regression — a straight-line/hyperplane boundary. It has nothing in common with a tree, CNN, or clustering algorithm.

mcqs.question: Why does stacking multiple neural network layers with no non-linear activation between them fail to add expressive power?
options: Because the layers run out of weights to learn
Because a stack of purely linear transformations collapses mathematically into a single linear transformation
Because backpropagation cannot compute gradients through linear layers
mcqs.explanation: Composing linear functions produces another linear function — no matter how many layers you stack, the whole network is still equivalent to one linear layer without a non-linearity in between. Gradients through linear layers are trivial to compute, and overfitting isn't the mechanism here.

mcqs.question: Why do very deep networks built entirely from sigmoid activations often fail to train their earliest layers?
options: Sigmoid activations use too much memory
Sigmoid only works for classification, not regression
Sigmoid's saturated regions produce near-zero gradients that shrink further as they're multiplied backward through many layers
mcqs.explanation: Sigmoid saturates for large-magnitude inputs, producing a near-zero local gradient; backpropagation multiplies these small gradients across many layers, shrinking the signal to nearly nothing by the time it reaches early layers — the vanishing-gradient problem. Sigmoid is fully differentiable and isn't restricted to classification.
